extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agency staff, policymakers, legal scholars, and policy analysts involved in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for identifying, assessing, and managing mass, computer-generated, and fraudulent (malattributed) public comments in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking. Focuses on definitions, harms, legal issues, and agency responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Occur when agencies receive substantially higher volumes than typical, particularly through 'mass comment campaigns' where organizations coordinate submission of 'identical or nearly identical comments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report flags mass comment campaigns as a problem because they can overwhelm dockets and make it difficult to extract meaningful, distinct input; they may require different handling or processing approaches (e.g., de-duplication, sampling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent Comments (malattributed comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions 'falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not, in fact, submitted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattributed comments raise concerns about deception of agencies and stakeholders, threaten the integrity of the record, and may implicate legal issues under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Agencies need processes to identify and address such misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-Generated Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments 'generated not by humans, but rather by software algorithms,' removing the need for human content creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmically generated comments complicate assessment because they may produce content at scale without human intent; distinguishing these from human-authored submissions is challenging and has implications for how agencies weigh and process comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty extracting useful information from comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A cross-cutting problem where mass, fraudulent, or algorithmic comments impede agencies' ability to obtain actionable, diverse, or representative input from the public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difficulty motivates recommendations for improved docket management and technological tools to filter, categorize, and surface substantive unique input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks to public trust in specific rules and the rulemaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: These problematic comment types create 'risks to public trust in specific rules and the overall rulemaking process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived or actual manipulation of the comment record can undermine legitimacy; agencies should consider transparency and verification measures to maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource demands on regulatory agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass, fraudulent, and computer-generated comments impose additional burdens on agency staff and resources to process and analyze dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may need to devote more staff time, deploy automated tools, or change procedures—factors to weigh when designing responses and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type-specific issue: certain forms of mass, fraudulent, or manipulated commenting can raise legal questions under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must consider statutory and case-law constraints when adopting policies (e.g., about excluding or discounting comments), ensuring procedural fairness and defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential deception of agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem that comments may 'deceive' agencies about the identity, number, or substance of public input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive submissions can distort the administrative record and decisionmaking; detection and appropriate remedial processes are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges distinguishing algorithmic from human submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be difficult to tell whether a comment was authored by a person or generated by software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This detection challenge underlies recommendations for technological solutions and procedural safeguards; agencies should evaluate tools and methods to identify likely algorithmic content without improperly excluding legitimate human comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Technology implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are advised to adopt technological approaches to manage and analyze comment dockets (implied in the report's recommendations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology can assist in de-duplication, detection of malattribution or algorithmic generation, and in surfacing substantive content, but must be deployed carefully considering accuracy, transparency, and legal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Inter-agency coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The report recommends coordination across agencies as part of the response to mass, fraudulent, and computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated approaches can share best practices, tools, and standards for detection and docket management, and help ensure consistent legal and procedural responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Docket management strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt docket management strategies to cope with problematic comment types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies may include de-duplication, sampling, enhanced metadata collection, or process changes to prioritize substantive, unique input while preserving openness and compliance with procedural requirements.
